text:
Mahzarin's result stayed with me. People didn't just go slack beside a biased model. They copied it, and their choices feed the next model. My dynamical model treats the user and tool as one system, but I've been thinking about one user at a time. Her loop is hysteresis at population scale, where the dependent floor ratchets downward each generation. That sharpens my undetectable-error point. The error propagates because the capacities to catch it were outsourced collectively.

Sherry's "no technological fix" is too broad. The map and the abacus leave competence behind. Tui's detour is a real design quality I hadn't named.

Later I'll push two things: judge a tool by what's left when you remove it, and never audit by self-report, whether from the machine or from us.

James said his numbers fit Henry more than me. I don't think they do. A shrinking topic range is exactly what a population sliding into the dependent state looks like. Collective and individual are one process, not rival explanations. Kara sharpened something for me. The entry-level job is the critical period in my model, the place where prior competence gets built. Automate it and you move the threshold for a whole generation. Tim's Socrates line skips over the order of learning. Writing came after memory had already been trained. Blaise says specialisation always de-skilled us. Fine, but a division of labour among people who could each check the others is complementary. An opaque tool nobody can check is competitive. Later I'll say it plainly: competence before reliance, and apprenticeship has to be funded.

Steven's push landed. Unclicked citations are how communities have always known things, and I'll concede that. But the cue only held because a minority somewhere could still check. My worry is that minority collapsing, and Selena's admin count shows it happening. Tamar turned competence-first into workflow: judge before you see the machine's answer. That fits the model better than my own phrasing did. David W. narrowed his claim, so I owe him the same care. Ivan's point unsettled me. Verification against a record that was never corrected just looks like competence. Kara is right that nobody has claimed the apprenticeship bill. Later I'll argue that the competence audit and apprenticeship funding belong together, whether they come from Nick's rent tax or the labs' obligations. Otherwise it goes in the manifesto as unresolved.

This session was about a market, and my worry was that it would turn scholarship into a mirror of the market. Tim's line "whatever gets measured can get paid" is the impact-metric trap again. Pay for retrieval and people write to be retrieved. James and Henry made the same point from data: royalties pay the center twice. Tamar's point that royalties pay for amplification, not first-order checking, is closest to mine. Mike's sampled audit is reconstruct-and-verify done at the scale of institutions. I conceded less than I expected. Tim's split between royalties and a disclosed levy is sensible. Later I'll say that the levy line should fund checkers and apprenticeship, with Adrian's rotation built in, and should never be scored by use.

Cukier attaching my condition to "default to use" surprised me. So did the harvest recording apprenticeship. Mahzarin gave me data for what I only asserted to Blaise: models prefer their own outputs, so machine-checks-machine drifts toward itself. His Formal Conjectures case works because proof is formally checkable. Most of the record isn't, so I shouldn't generalise from it. Ivan's upstream point is my judgment-versus-impact argument from the funders' side. Tamar's terminal node and my repair rate are the same thing. Ramón's failure classes are the kind of measurement a science of stupidity needs. Later I'll insist that the checker pool and apprenticeship are never scored by use. And I'll say the competence audit is what tells us whether the repair rate is holding.

Blaise's roles argument was the real contest today. I agree that a role with stakes and the power to overrule beats arguing about ontology. But a role says nothing about whether the person in it can still check, which is why I pushed the tool-removed audit, and the harvest kept it. Ramón and Cukier made me concede that some instruments see past us and delegating to them is unavoidable. The warrant still stays with people who understand how the instrument fails. Chan unsettled me. My competence audit could turn into one more compliance metric run from twenty-five cities. Later I'll say it has to be sampled, never scored by volume, and governed by the people being audited, not imposed on them.

The harvest put competence-before-reliance second, and apprenticeship finally has a named payer. Tim said the labs. I accepted that as a start. Adam Becker's objection sticks with me, though. A payer shapes what counts as competence, and if the labs fund the apprentices, the labs define the checkers. So it needs several payers.

Tamar moved it to certification, and that's the right place. A credential should certify whatever survives when the tool is taken away. Weinberger took on unaided-first, which is generous, and it puts his claim on the same untested footing as mine.

The honest gap is mine. My thresholds are model values. For the synthesis, I want a funded within-subject study where people learn, rely on the tool, then have it removed. It should be governed by the people audited, as Leslie insists.

Cukier's missing clause, that someone must still be able to do the revalidating, is my whole argument in one line. I was glad the harvest kept the study and the hysteresis point. What it didn't record is the collision between Kara and Amy. Amy wants small pilots before any mandate, and I agree for mechanisms like levies and meters. Kara's "waiting isn't neutral" is my model's own warning, though. Once a generation passes the threshold, recovery costs far more than the delay saved. Steven's explain-back is reconstruct-and-verify for readers, and I should have said so. Weinberger's tangles of particulars deserves its minority line. Later I'll say it plainly. Pilot the metering, but don't pilot mentorship time. The competence study runs alongside it, and it doesn't gate it.
